The Story of Prince Lakuch

I bow to Lord Jinendra, who sees and knows the world and beyond through pure omniscient knowledge, and I write the story of Prince Lakuch, who was devoted to dharma.

King Dhanvarma and Queen Dhanshri of Ujjain had a son named Lakuch. Lakuch was very proud, but also brave. People compared him to a cloud, for he would extinguish the fire of his enemies' pride. Victory over enemies was as easy for him as using his left hand.

The mlechchha king Kalamegh had once attacked Ujjain, causing great loss of life and wealth to the people of Avanti. Lakuch launched a counter-attack on Kalamegh's land. After a fierce battle on both sides, the goddess of victory sat in Lakuch's lap. Lakuch brought Kalamegh bound before his father. Dhanvarma was greatly pleased by his son's valour. In his joy, he offered Lakuch a boon, leaving the choice to his son.

Receiving permission to choose as he wished, Lakuch's eyes wandered astray. He began to misuse his boon. His gaze turned toward adultery. Virtuous women of good families began to fall prey to him. Their dharma was being corrupted. Many chaste women even committed suicide to protect their honour from this sinner. The people were distressed. They could not even complain to the king, for the prince's spies were spread throughout every corner of Ujjain. Whoever spoke or even thought against the prince was immediately put to death.

In that city lived a merchant named Pungal, whose wife was Nagdatta. Nagdatta was very beautiful. One day, the sinful Lakuch cast his eyes upon her. There was no delay — he immediately possessed her, satisfying his base desire. Pungal was burned from head to toe by this vileness. The fire of anger spread through every fibre of his being. Helpless due to the prince's terror, he could do nothing. But he waited eagerly for the day when he could take full revenge.

Eventually, Lakuch's sins caught up with him. His immoral conduct led to his downfall. He lost his father's favour, his power, and ultimately his life. Through the ripening of his heavy sins, he fell into a lower birth and suffered greatly.

This story teaches that power without moral restraint leads to destruction. Prince Lakuch had everything — bravery, intelligence, his father's love, and a boon of his choice. But he misused his power for sensual gratification, violating the dharma of countless women. His actions brought suffering to many and ultimately led to his own ruin. The wise should understand that true strength lies not in the power to harm others but in the self-control to refrain from doing so. Those in positions of authority must exercise their power with moral responsibility.
